risk_review.notes: Reviewed all nine steps and the exact quaternion cover, symmetric-power representation, finite spin matrices, componentwise rotation action and maximal directional domains. C is orthogonal with determinant one; the Pauli subgroups correspond to axes (-k,-j,-i), and Rodrigues conjugation gives rho(A_i(t))=R_i(t) with the stated sign. Finite spectral matrix projections commute with the spatial flow, hence its projections; bounded S_i permits the product-flow lemma on D(L_i). Continuity follows from matrix norm continuity plus spatial strong continuity and the unitary bound. s=0 is trivial, and the central sign is (-1)^(2s). AC implies the additional dependent-choice supplier hypothesis. No physical premise is used.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Use the notation of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-strongly-continuous-rotation-action]]: $S^2$, the polar measure $\sigma$ with
$\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, the Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$, the complete orthonormal family $(Y_{lm})$, the blocks
$V_l$, the finite span $H$, the spaces $H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ of complex harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree
$l$, the restriction maps $\mathrm{res}_l$, and the unitary action $U(R)F=\text{class of }\tilde F(R^{-1}\cdot)$
of $SO(3)$. Fix $\hbar>0$ and for $i=1,2,3$ define the rotation matrices
$$R_1(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos t&-\sin t\\0&\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_2(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&0&\sin t\\0&1&0\\-\sin t&0&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_3(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t&0\\ \sin t&\cos t&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$
put $U_i(t):=U(R_i(t))$. Let $L_z$ denote the diagonal operator of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]], set $S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$, $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$,
and define
$$L_3:=L_z,\qquad L_1:=U(S)^{-1}L_zU(S),\qquad L_2:=U(W)^{-1}L_zU(W),$$
with domains $D(L_1)=U(S)^{-1}D(L_z)$, $D(L_2)=U(W)^{-1}D(L_z)$ and $D(L_3)=D(L_z)$.
Here $e^{-itL_z/\hbar}$ is the explicit diagonal unitary sending $Y_{lm}$ to $e^{-itm}Y_{lm}$;
$e^{-itL_1/\hbar}$ and $e^{-itL_2/\hbar}$ mean its conjugates by $U(S)$ and $U(W)$, respectively.
The proof identifies these operators with the complete strong derivative generators, so this construction
has the same generator meaning without an appeal to an unrestricted spectral or Stone theorem. For a polynomial $p$ put
$$D_ip:=(x\times\nabla p)_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\partial_kp,$$
where $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(1,2,3)\mapsto(i,j,k)$ and is $0$ when two indices
coincide. Then:

(a) each $L_i$ is a self-adjoint operator on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with $U(R_i(t))=e^{-itL_i/\hbar}$ for all real
$t$; the finite span $H$ is contained in $D(L_i)$ and is a core of $L_i$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);
and for $F\in V_l$ with polynomial representative $p_F\in H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ one has
$$L_iF=\mathrm{res}_l(-i\hbar\,D_ip_F),$$
that is, $(L_iF)(\Omega)=-i\hbar\,D_ip_F(\Omega)$ for $\sigma$-almost every $\Omega\in S^2$; in particular
$L_iY_{lm}\in V_l$ for all $l,m$ and $L_iH\subseteq H$;

(b) on $H$ the operators satisfy the commutation relations
$$L_iL_j-L_jL_i=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k;$$

(c) $L_3=L_z$ as self-adjoint operators (equal domains and equal action); in particular $L_3Y_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$, so that
$L_3$ is diagonal in the basis $(Y_{lm})$, and for every $F\in H$ and chart point $(\theta,\varphi)$ one has $(L_3F)(\theta,\varphi)=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi)$;

(d) rotational conjugation identifies the domains: with the two quarter-turn rotations
$S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$ and $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$ one has
$$U(S)L_1U(S)^{-1}=L_3,\qquad U(W)L_2U(W)^{-1}=L_3,$$
as self-adjoint operators, and consequently $U(S)D(L_1)=D(L_3)$ and $U(W)D(L_2)=D(L_3)$: the three domains
are unitarily identified.

All assertions are mathematical statements about operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$; no physical interpretation of
the generators as angular momentum is asserted, and no measurement postulate is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix a real parameter $\hbar>0$. Let
$(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,-l\le m\le l}$ be the complete orthonormal family of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ constructed in
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]], and let
$H:=\operatorname{span}\{Y_{lm}:-l\le m\le l,\ l\in\mathbb N\}$ be its algebraic (finite) span. Define operators
$A$ and $L_z$ on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ by the diagonal lemma
[[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]]:

$$D(A):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}l^2(l+1)^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad AF:=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$
$$D(L_z):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}m^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad L_zF:=\sum_{l,m}\hbar m\,\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$

the sums being in the Hilbert-space norm ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Finally, for $F$ in the finite span
$H$ and a chart point $(\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ write $F(\theta,\varphi)$ for the value of $F$
at $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)$ and put

$$(\mathcal S F)(\theta,\varphi):=-\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta\bigl(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta F\bigr)(\theta,\varphi) -\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi^2F(\theta,\varphi),\qquad (\mathcal D F)(\theta,\varphi):=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi),$$

where the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

(a) $A$ and $L_z$ are self-adjoint operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with the displayed domains; on $Y_{lm}$ they
act by $AY_{lm}=l(l+1)Y_{lm}$ and $L_zY_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]); $A$ is nonnegative, $\langle AF,F\rangle\ge0$, and
$A\mathbf 1=0$;

(b) $H$ is a core of $A$ and of $L_z$: the finite truncations
$F_N:=\sum_{l\le N}\sum_{m}\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$ of an element $F$ of $D(A)$ satisfy $F_N\to F$ and
$AF_N\to AF$ in $L^2$, and analogously with $L_z$;

(c) for every $F\in H$ and every chart point with $\sin\theta\ne0$,
$$\mathcal S F(\theta,\varphi)=(AF)(\theta,\varphi),\qquad \mathcal D F(\theta,\varphi)=(L_zF)(\theta,\varphi);$$

(d) for every $l$ the orthogonal projection $P_l$ of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ onto the $(2l+1)$-dimensional span of
$Y_{l,-l},\dots,Y_{ll}$ reduces both $A$ and $L_z$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]), i.e. $P_lA\subseteq AP_l$
and $P_lL_z\subseteq L_zP_l$; consequently $A$ and $L_z$ commute on the finite span $H$, and for every $F\in D(A)$ with
$\sum_{l,m}\bigl(l(l+1)\hbar m\bigr)^2|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty$ one has
$AL_zF=L_zAF=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\hbar m\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$. Writing $c_{lm}=\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle$ and $\lambda_l=l(l+1)$, the maximal product domains are $D(AL_z)=\{F\in L^2:\sum_{l,m}(\lambda_l\hbar m)^2|c_{lm}|^2<\infty\}$ and $D(L_zA)=D(A)\cap D(AL_z)$. Thus this is exactly the common domain $D(AL_z)\cap D(L_zA)=D(L_zA)$, while the two maximal product domains need not coincide. The product-weight condition alone does not imply $F\in D(A)$: the vector with coefficients $c_{l0}=1/l$ for $l\ge1$ and all other coefficients zero belongs to $L^2$, has zero product weight, but does not belong to $D(A)$. The product-weight condition is not automatic for all $F\in D(A)\cap D(L_z)$.

The differential expression $\mathcal S$ is evaluated only away from the poles, where the coordinate formulas are
defined; no claim is made about a maximal differential operator on all of $S^2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]) and let $(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l}$ be the
functions of [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] ([[def-complex-exponential]]).
Then $(Y_{lm})$ is a complete orthonormal family of the complex Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]):
the family is orthonormal, and if $F\in L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ satisfies
$\int_{S^2}F\overline{Y_{lm}}\,d\sigma=0$ for all $l\ge0$ and $-l\le m\le l$, then $F=0$ almost everywhere.
Consequently every $F$ has the expansion
$$F=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=-l}^{l}\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},\qquad \|F\|^2=\sum_{l,m}|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2,$$
with $\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle=\int_{S^2}F\overline{Y_{lm}}\,d\sigma$ and finite-subset-net convergence
([[thm-parseval-equivalences-for-a-complete-orthonormal-family]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be an endomorphism. The endomorphism $T$ is **self-adjoint** when

$$T^*=T,$$

and **normal** when

$$TT^*=T^*T,$$

where $T^*$ is the adjoint from
[[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]].

Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

- **(W1)** $0_V \in W$;
- **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies
  $u + v \in W$;
- **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: $\lambda \in F$ and
  $v \in W$ imply $\lambda v \in W$.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]].

derivations.claim: [Invariance and finite self-adjointness] Fix $l$; by [F1] $L_{i}V_{l}\subseteq V_{l}$, and by [F3] applied to the invariant finite-dimensional subspace $V_{l}\subset L^{2}(S^{2},\sigma)$ the restriction $L_{i}|_{V_{l}}$ is a self-adjoint endomorphism of $V_{l}$; by [F1] and [F2], $L_{3}Y_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$ for every $m$ with $|m|\le l$, which is (a).

[Angular momentum relations on the block] Put $J_{i}:=(1/\hbar)L_{i}|_{V_{l}}$; by step 1.1 the $J_{i}$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_{l}$ and by [F1] they satisfy $[J_{i},J_{j}]=i\sum_{k}\varepsilon_{ijk}J_{k}$ on $V_{l}$; moreover $J^{2}:=\sum_{i}J_{i}^{2}$ commutes with each $J_{i}$ by [F4] clause (a), and the eigenvalues of $J_{3}$ on $V_{l}$, read in units of $\hbar$, are $-l,-l+1,\dots,l$, each simple by [F5].

[Finite span] Let $F\in H$; as a finite linear combination $F=\sum_{l,m}c_{lm}Y_{lm}$, the identities of step 3.1 apply to each term because $Y_{lm}\in V_{l}$, and $\sum_{i}L_{i}^{2}F=\sum_{l,m}c_{lm}\hbar^{2}l(l+1)Y_{lm}=\hbar^{2}AF$ by the diagonal definition of $A$ in [F2] and the linearity of the finite sums.

boundaries.evidence: The finite harmonic span permits F=0 with an empty finite expansion in step 4.1. Its harmonic sum, AF and all L_i^2F are zero by linearity, so the identity is 0=0. Each actual block V_l has dimension 2l+1>=1 by F2.
For l=0 step 3.1 gives J²=0 and step 1.1 gives L_3 Y_00=0; the degree-zero block lies in the finite span H of clause (c).
For l=1 step 3.1 gives ΣL_i²F=2ħ²F=ħ²·1·2·F on V_1.
Step 2.1 records the simple weight spectrum −l,…,l and step 3.1 identifies the single block of parameter l; no multiplicity is left undetermined.
The weight endpoints m=±l of V_l are included in the spectrum used in steps 1.1 and 3.1.
The statement assumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; the orthonormal basis (Y_lm) and the countable-data facts [F2],[F5] used in steps 1.1-3.1 rest on it.

Let $s\in\frac12\mathbb N=\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$, put $N:=2s\in\mathbb N$ and let
$V_s:=\mathbb C^{N+1}$ carry the standard inner product
$\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_k\overline{w_k}$, linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Write $(e_m)_{-s\le m\le s}$ for the standard basis, indexed so that
$e_m$ is the vector with entry $1$ in position $k=s-m$ and entry $0$ elsewhere; thus
$\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=1$ if $m=n$ and $\langle e_m,e_n\rangle=0$ otherwise. Define $\mathbb C$-linear maps
$J_z,J_+,J_-\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_s)$ by their values on this basis ([[def-linear-map]]):

$$J_ze_m:=m\,e_m,\qquad J_+e_m:=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}\,e_{m+1},\qquad J_-e_m:=\sqrt{(s+m)(s-m+1)}\,e_{m-1},$$

where $e_{s+1}:=0$ and $e_{-s-1}:=0$, and put

$$J_x:=\tfrac12(J_++J_-),\qquad J_y:=\tfrac1{2i}(J_+-J_-),\qquad J^2:=J_x^2+J_y^2+J_z^2 .$$

Then:

(a) $J_z$, $J_x$ and $J_y$ are self-adjoint endomorphisms of $V_s$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]), and $J_+^*=J_-$, $J_-^*=J_+$
([[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]]);

(b) on $V_s$ the commutators are

$$[J_z,J_+]=J_+,\qquad [J_z,J_-]=-J_-,\qquad [J_+,J_-]=2J_z,\qquad [J_x,J_y]=iJ_z,\qquad [J_y,J_z]=iJ_x,\qquad [J_z,J_x]=iJ_y ;$$

(c) $J^2=J_-J_++J_z^2+J_z=J_+J_-+J_z^2-J_z=s(s+1)I$, and $[J^2,J_z]=[J^2,J_\pm]=0$;

(d) the matrix elements of the raising operator are
$\|J_+e_m\|^2=(s-m)(s+m+1)$ and $\|J_-e_m\|^2=(s+m)(s-m+1)$, and
$\langle J_+e_m,e_{m+1}\rangle=\sqrt{(s-m)(s+m+1)}$, which is nonzero exactly when $m<s$;

(e) for $s=\tfrac12$, identify $V_{\frac12}=\mathbb C^2$ with the basis ordered as $(e_{\frac12},e_{-\frac12})$ and let

$$\sigma_x:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_y:=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\ i&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \sigma_z:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$$

be the Pauli matrices. Then $J_i=\tfrac12\sigma_i$ for $i=x,y,z$, $\sigma_x^2=\sigma_y^2=\sigma_z^2=I$,
$\sigma_x\sigma_y=i\sigma_z$, $\sigma_y\sigma_z=i\sigma_x$, $\sigma_z\sigma_x=i\sigma_y$, and consequently
$\sigma_i\sigma_j+\sigma_j\sigma_i=2\delta_{ij}I$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\sum_k\varepsilon_{ijk}\sigma_k$ for all $i,j$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $\varepsilon_{ijk}=0$ when two of $i,j,k$ coincide, and otherwise $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(x,y,z)\mapsto(i,j,k)$; the sum ranges over $k\in\{x,y,z\}$. The same convention with indices $1,2,3$ uses the order-preserving relabelling $(1,2,3)=(x,y,z)$.

All statements are finite-dimensional linear algebra: no physical interpretation of $J_x,J_y,J_z$ as angular momentum, and no measurement postulate, is asserted here.

**(a) Adopted model and state space.** Adopt the kinematics and
massive-particle model postulate P5 for a declared particle of mass parameter
$m>0$, spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and internal factor
assigned as in the identical-particle and spin postulate P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]]). Put $r:=2s+1$ and take
as the model's one-particle state space the complex Hilbert space
$$H_{s}:=L^{2}\bigl(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r}\bigr) =\Bigl\{f:\mathbb R^{3}\to\mathbb C^{r}\ \text{measurable}:\ \int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\|f(x)\|_{\mathbb C^{r}}^{2}\,dx<\infty\Bigr\}\Big/\!\sim,$$
the quotient by equality almost everywhere, with inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\sum_{l=1}^{r}f_{l}\overline{g_{l}}\,dx$
linear in the first argument ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]).
Thus an element of $H_{s}$ is a class of functions, not a function, and
pointwise values of a state are not defined; the position density is read from
the class through the observables of clause (b) and the observable and
probability postulate P2 ([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]). Its dimension
in the conventions of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)1
is $\ell^{-3/2}$ per component. P5 presents the same space as the completed
tensor product $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)\widehat\otimes\mathbb C^{r}$
with the spin factor carrying the representation of P6; the unitary
identification of the two descriptions and the componentwise reading of
componentwise operators are those of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] and
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]. The orthonormal
basis $(e_{m})_{m=-s,\dots,s}$ of $\mathbb C^{r}$ is the basis fixed by P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii)).

**(b) Position and momentum.** The model's $j$-th position and $k$-th momentum
are the componentwise operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a): for
$f=(f_{l})$, restricted to the classes with $x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ respectively
with $D_{k}f_{l}\in L^{2}$ for all $l$,
$$(Q_{j}f)_{l}(x):=x_{j}f_{l}(x),\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
with $D_{k}$ the weak derivative and $\hbar$ the action constant of
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. These are the scalar operators of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]] applied
componentwise. The model assigns to $(Q_{j},\mathrm m)$ and to
$(P_{k},\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})$ the status of assigned sharp observables in
the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]
clause (a), with the units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4; both are densely defined and self-adjoint by
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]] clause (a). On the
Schwartz core they satisfy the componentwise canonical commutation relations,
and they commute with the internal-factor operators of clause (c) in the sense
of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]] clauses (a),(c).

**(c) Internal factor.** For $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ let $S_{i}=\hbar J_{i}$ be the
self-adjoint endomorphisms of $\mathbb C^{r}$ of the spin assignment P6
([[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii),
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]), and let the model read
them on $H_{s}$ as the matrix actions
$$(S_{i}f)_{l}:=\hbar\sum_{m=1}^{r}(J_{i})_{lm}f_{m}\qquad(l=1,\dots,r),$$
that is, as the amplifications $I\otimes S_{i}$ under the tensor
identification of clause (a) ([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-ccr-and-internal-factor-commutation]]
clause (d)). Their declared unit is the unit of action ([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]
clause (d)4). The factor is internal bookkeeping: it is not a spatial
coordinate, not a rotating body and not a relativistic spinor, and the model
assigns no position or worldline to it.

**(d) Momentum-space representative.** With $U^{(s)}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] for $r=2s+1$, the
**momentum-space representative** of a preparation vector $\psi\in H_{s}$ is
$\psi_{p}:=U^{(s)}\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3},dp;\mathbb C^{r})$; for a
Schwartz class $\psi$ it is the componentwise Fourier transform
$$(\psi_{p})_{l}(p)=(2\pi\hbar)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}e^{-ip\cdot x/\hbar}\psi_{l}(x)\,dx,$$
and its dimension is $(\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})^{-3/2}$ per component
([[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] clause (d)2). By
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-momentum-representation]] clause (b), $P_{k}$ acts on the
momentum representative by multiplication by $p_{k}$; this is the model's
momentum reading and no measured momentum distribution is identified with
$|\psi_{p}|^{2}$ by this definition.

**(e) Frame reading.** The model's inertial frames are the global coordinate
charts of P5; frame changes are the Galilean transformations of P5, with
parameters and units as in [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. This
definition uses P5's frame class only. The transformation law of state
representatives under a change of inertial frame is a derived statement about
the model's operators and is established by the covariance theorems of this
page for translations and boosts; it is not an additional assumption of this
definition, and no Lorentz transformation law is claimed.

**(f) Status.** Clauses (a)-(e) record the readings of P1, P2, P5 and P6 in the
terminology of this page and fix the objects used by its theorems. They assert
no time evolution beyond what the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4 assigns
([[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]]
clause (iv)), no preparation or apparatus model, no detection model and no
empirical result. Massless particles, relativistic matter, radiation, singular
or unbounded potentials and boundary or confined realizations are separate
model assumptions with their own domains and self-adjointness statements; none
is obtained from this definition.

**(a) Adopted readings.** Adopt the state and composition postulate P1, the
observable and probability postulate P2, the autonomous-dynamics postulate P4,
the kinematics and massive-particle model postulate P5 and the internal-factor
assignment of the identical-particle and spin postulate P6, all read for the
spin-$s$ model of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] with
mass parameter $m>0$, spin label $s\in\{0,\tfrac12,1,\tfrac32,\dots\}$ and
$r=2s+1$
([[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-nonrelativistic-kinematics-and-massive-particle]],
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]],
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]],
[[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]]). Let
$H_{s}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the model's state space with
componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$, and let $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ be its
componentwise Schwartz class
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]]). Units are
those of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]; the unit of angular
momentum is the unit of action (J$\,$s).

**(b) Orbital angular momentum.** For $i=1,2,3$ let $L_{i}$ be the
self-adjoint operator on $H_{s}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-symmetries-rotation-generators-on-schwartz-classes]], the Stone
generator of the coordinate rotation group $t\mapsto U(R_{i}(t))$, so that
$U(R_{i}(t))=e^{-itL_{i}/\hbar}$ and, on the Schwartz class,
$$L_{i}\psi=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}\,Q_{j}P_{k}\psi$$
([[lem-nrqm-symmetries-rotation-generators-on-schwartz-classes]] clause (b),
[[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]). The model reads
$(L_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an **assigned sharp observable**, called the
$i$-th **orbital angular momentum** of the model, with outcome law
$\mu^{L_{i}}_{\rho}$ in a preparation $\rho$
([[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clauses (a),(b),
[[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]). The operators
$L_{i}$ act on the spatial factor only; their reading on the angular degrees
of freedom is the one supplied by the sphere operators
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-orbital-self-adjoint-generators]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]], and the finite-blocks identity
$\sum_{i}L_{i}^{2}F=\hbar^{2}l(l+1)F$ on the harmonic span is the content of a
separate lemma of this page
([[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-orbital-casimir-identity]]).

**(c) Spin angular momentum.** Let $S_{i}=\hbar J_{i}$ be the internal
operators of [[def-nrqm-kinematics-framework-massive-spin-s-model]] clause
(c), the matrix actions $\bigl(S_{i}f\bigr)_{l}=\hbar\sum_{m}(J_{i})_{lm}f_{m}$
of the self-adjoint matrices of
[[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]]. The model reads
$(S_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an assigned sharp observable, the $i$-th **spin
angular momentum**; on the internal factor,
$$[S_{i},S_{j}]=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}S_{k},\qquad S^{2}:=S_{x}^{2}+S_{y}^{2}+S_{z}^{2}=\hbar^{2}s(s+1)I$$
([[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clauses (a),(b),(c),
[[post-nrqm-framework-identical-particles-and-spin]] clause (ii)). The
**ladder** operators $S_{\pm}:=S_{x}\pm iS_{y}$ and the finite projections on
the basis vectors $e_{m}$ are structural objects of the internal factor, not
assigned sharp observables, and $S_{\pm}$ are not self-adjoint. For $s=\tfrac12$
one has $S_{i}=\tfrac{\hbar}{2}\sigma_{i}$ in the Pauli matrices
([[prop-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-finite-spin-matrices]] clause (e)). The internal
factor is a finite-dimensional bookkeeping factor: it is not a spatial
coordinate, not a rotating body and not a relativistic spinor, and the model
assigns no position or worldline to it.

**(d) Total angular momentum.** For each $i$ let
$$J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}:=L_{i}+S_{i},\qquad D(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}):=D(L_{i}),$$
the self-adjoint sum of
[[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-su2-lift-of-the-rotation-action]] clause (c)
(well defined because $S_{i}$ is bounded and strongly commutes with $L_{i}$;
[[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-product-flow-generator]] clause (a),
[[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). The model reads
$(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ as an assigned sharp observable, the
$i$-th **total angular momentum**; its flow is the coordinate subgroup
$t\mapsto U_{s}(A_{i}(t))$ of the lifted rotation action, using the physical-axes cover $\rho(W)=C^{-1}\rho_0(W)C$ defined in that lemma (rather than the literal quaternion-coordinate cover $\rho_0$),
$U_{s}(A_{i}(t))=e^{-itJ_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}}/\hbar}$
([[lem-nrqm-angular-momentum-su2-lift-of-the-rotation-action]] clauses (b),(c)).

**(e) Status and scope.** Clauses (a)-(d) fix the angular momentum vocabulary
of this page within P1, P2, P4, P5 and P6 and the cited readings. No new
physical assumption is added; in particular no magnetic coupling, no
spin-orbit interaction, no SU(2) gauge structure and no anomaly is
introduced. Whether a laboratory angular momentum measurement is described by
one of the assigned pairs $(L_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$, $(S_{i},\mathrm{J\,s})$ or
$(J_{i}^{\mathrm{tot}},\mathrm{J\,s})$ is a tested identification with
uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7, not a
consequence of this definition; no measurement procedure, apparatus,
resolution or empirical value is supplied here. Antiunitary symmetries,
superselection rules and symmetries of preparations as opposed to dynamics
are outside the definition.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $E_{A,x}(B):=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ be its scalar measures ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ say that $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of $A$ when $Ax=\lambda x$ for some nonzero $x\in D(A)$, the domain-restricted reading of [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]. Then:

(a) The orthogonal projection $E_A(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection of $H$ onto the eigenspace $\ker(A-\lambda)=\{x\in D(A):Ax=\lambda x\}$; in particular $E_A(\{\lambda\})\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, that is every self-adjoint positive trace-class $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)), the number $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(\{\lambda\}))$ is the weight that the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ assigns to the singleton $\{\lambda\}$: it vanishes for every $\rho$ whenever $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, and it equals $1$ for the pure state $T_{u,u}$ of every unit eigenvector $u\in\ker(A-\lambda)$.

(c) If $A$ has no eigenvalues at all, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=0$ for every density operator $\rho$ and every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: the scalar law of every state carries no point mass, while its values on general Borel sets remain $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(B))$.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. **Density operators.** Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space. A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a) ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). The **state space** of $H$ is the set of all density operators on $H$ and is denoted
$$D(H):=\{\rho:\rho\ \text{is a density operator on}\ H\}.$$
An element of $D(H)$ is called a **state** of $H$ in the mathematical sense fixed here.

**Pure states.** A state $\rho\in D(H)$ is **pure** when there is a unit vector $u\in S(H)$ with
$$\rho=T_{u,u},\qquad T_{u,u}x=\langle x,u\rangle u\quad(x\in H),$$
where $T_{u,u}$ is the rank-one operator of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] and $S(H)$ is the unit sphere of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. By [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] the pure states are exactly the Hilbert orthogonal projections of $H$ with one-dimensional range, and the map
$$j:R(H)\longrightarrow D(H),\qquad j([\psi]):=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
on the ray space $R(H)$, with $\nu$ the normalization map, is well defined and injective with image the set of pure states. A state is **mixed** when it is not pure. For a nonzero vector $\psi$ the **normalized rank-one operator of $\psi$** is
$$\widehat\rho(\psi):=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\operatorname{tr}(T_{\psi,\psi})},$$
which equals $T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}$; thus $\widehat\rho(\psi)$ is the pure state of the ray $[\psi]$, and the vector $\psi$ enters only through its ray.

**Purity.** For $\rho\in D(H)$ the operator $\rho^{2}$ is self-adjoint, positive and trace class: it is self-adjoint by the adjoint algebra of [[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]], positive because $\langle\rho^{2}x,x\rangle=\langle\rho x,\rho x\rangle\ge0$, and trace class because $\rho$ is a bounded trace-class operator and the trace-class operators form a two-sided ideal ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]] clauses 1 and 2). The **purity** of $\rho$ is the real number
$$\mathcal P(\rho):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho^{2})\in\mathbb R.$$
The numerical range of the purity and the equivalence of purity with purity of the state are established by the purity criterion of this page; this definition records the object only.

**Scope.** This definition fixes the mathematical state space of a Hilbert space together with the pure states, the mixed states, the normalized rank-one operator of a nonzero vector and the purity functional. The cited rank-one calculus and the density-operator expansion assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and the definition is read under that assumption. It asserts no dynamics, no measurement, no probability law and no physical interpretation, and it introduces no new assumptions beyond the cited mathematics and that choice hypothesis. In particular, whether a given physical preparation is described by a pure or a mixed state is a question about the model's assignments, not about this definition.

$$D(H)=\{\rho:\rho\ \text{is a density operator on}\ H\}$$
of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]]: the self-adjoint positive trace-class operators on $H$ of trace one. A **state** of the system is an element of $D(H)$; this is the geometry vocabulary for the general preparations of clause (iii) of the state postulate. The model's adopted assignment of a state to each preparation is not produced by this definition; it is the content of that postulate.

$$j:R(H)\to D(H),\qquad j([\psi])=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)},$$
is a bijection of the ray space onto the set of pure states; and by clause (ii) of the state postulate the pure preparations are the unit rays of $H$, so the model's pure preparations are exactly its pure states.

$$\widehat\rho(\psi)=\frac{T_{\psi,\psi}}{\|\psi\|^{2}}=T_{\nu(\psi),\nu(\psi)}\in D(H),$$
which by [[lem-nrqm-state-geometry-ray-to-rank-one-projection]] depends only on the ray $[\psi]$; clause (ii) of the state postulate assigns the same operator to the pure preparation $[\psi]$. The zero vector is excluded here because $\|\psi\|^{-1}$ is defined only for $\psi\ne0$; no state is assigned to it, in agreement with the state postulate.

derivations.claim: [Fibrewise spectral measure and law of $S_{n}$] By step 1.1 the matrix $n\cdot J$ has the simple eigenvalues $m=-s,\dots,s$; let $P_{n,m}$ be the fibrewise action on $H_{s}$ of the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb C^{r}$ onto the eigenline of $n\cdot J$ with eigenvalue $m$; each $P_{n,m}$ is an orthogonal projection on $H_{s}$, $P_{n,m}P_{n,m'}=0$ for $m\ne m'$, $\sum_{m}P_{n,m}=I$ fibrewise, and $S_{n}=\sum_{m}\hbar mP_{n,m}$ as bounded operators; consequently $\ker(S_{n}-\hbar m)=\operatorname{ran}P_{n,m}$ because a class $f$ satisfies $\hbar(n\cdot J)f(x)=\hbar mf(x)$ for almost every $x$ exactly when $f(x)$ lies in the $m$-eigenline almost everywhere; by [F4] applied to the self-adjoint $S_{n}$ of [F3], $E_{S_{n}}(\{\hbar m\})=P_{n,m}$ and $\mu^{S_{n}}_{\psi}(\{\hbar m\})=\|P_{n,m}\psi\|^{2}=\langle P_{n,m}\psi,\psi\rangle$ for every unit $\psi$; since $\sum_{m}P_{n,m}=I$, the law is concentrated on $\hbar\{-s,\dots,s\}$, which is (a).

This is (b).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Use the notation of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-strongly-continuous-rotation-action]]: $S^2$, the polar measure $\sigma$ with
$\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, the Hilbert space $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$, the complete orthonormal family $(Y_{lm})$, the blocks
$V_l$, the finite span $H$, the spaces $H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ of complex harmonic homogeneous polynomials of degree
$l$, the restriction maps $\mathrm{res}_l$, and the unitary action $U(R)F=\text{class of }\tilde F(R^{-1}\cdot)$
of $SO(3)$. Fix $\hbar>0$ and for $i=1,2,3$ define the rotation matrices
$$R_1(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos t&-\sin t\\0&\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_2(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&0&\sin t\\0&1&0\\-\sin t&0&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_3(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t&0\\ \sin t&\cos t&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$
put $U_i(t):=U(R_i(t))$. Let $L_z$ denote the diagonal operator of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]], set $S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$, $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$,
and define
$$L_3:=L_z,\qquad L_1:=U(S)^{-1}L_zU(S),\qquad L_2:=U(W)^{-1}L_zU(W),$$
with domains $D(L_1)=U(S)^{-1}D(L_z)$, $D(L_2)=U(W)^{-1}D(L_z)$ and $D(L_3)=D(L_z)$.
Here $e^{-itL_z/\hbar}$ is the explicit diagonal unitary sending $Y_{lm}$ to $e^{-itm}Y_{lm}$;
$e^{-itL_1/\hbar}$ and $e^{-itL_2/\hbar}$ mean its conjugates by $U(S)$ and $U(W)$, respectively.
The proof identifies these operators with the complete strong derivative generators, so this construction
has the same generator meaning without an appeal to an unrestricted spectral or Stone theorem. For a polynomial $p$ put
$$D_ip:=(x\times\nabla p)_i=\sum_{j,k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}\,x_j\,\partial_kp,$$
where $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ is the sign of the permutation $(1,2,3)\mapsto(i,j,k)$ and is $0$ when two indices
coincide. Then:

(a) each $L_i$ is a self-adjoint operator on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with $U(R_i(t))=e^{-itL_i/\hbar}$ for all real
$t$; the finite span $H$ is contained in $D(L_i)$ and is a core of $L_i$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]);
and for $F\in V_l$ with polynomial representative $p_F\in H_l^{\mathrm{pol}}$ one has
$$L_iF=\mathrm{res}_l(-i\hbar\,D_ip_F),$$
that is, $(L_iF)(\Omega)=-i\hbar\,D_ip_F(\Omega)$ for $\sigma$-almost every $\Omega\in S^2$; in particular
$L_iY_{lm}\in V_l$ for all $l,m$ and $L_iH\subseteq H$;

(b) on $H$ the operators satisfy the commutation relations
$$L_iL_j-L_jL_i=i\hbar\sum_{k=1}^3\varepsilon_{ijk}L_k;$$

(c) $L_3=L_z$ as self-adjoint operators (equal domains and equal action); in particular $L_3Y_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$, so that
$L_3$ is diagonal in the basis $(Y_{lm})$, and for every $F\in H$ and chart point $(\theta,\varphi)$ one has $(L_3F)(\theta,\varphi)=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi)$;

(d) rotational conjugation identifies the domains: with the two quarter-turn rotations
$S:=R_2(-\pi/2)$ and $W:=R_1(\pi/2)$ one has
$$U(S)L_1U(S)^{-1}=L_3,\qquad U(W)L_2U(W)^{-1}=L_3,$$
as self-adjoint operators, and consequently $U(S)D(L_1)=D(L_3)$ and $U(W)D(L_2)=D(L_3)$: the three domains
are unitarily identified.

All assertions are mathematical statements about operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$; no physical interpretation of
the generators as angular momentum is asserted, and no measurement postulate is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $P_l$ be the Legendre polynomials of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-legendre-rodrigues-equation]], and for $l\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le m\le l$ define the
function $w_{lm}:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ by

$$w_{lm}(t):=(-1)^m(1-t^2)^{m/2}\,\frac{d^m}{dt^m}P_l(t),$$

where $(1-t^2)^{1/2}>0$ denotes the nonnegative square root. Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ and let the angle coordinates be $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$
([[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]],
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]). The image of $\Phi$ is
$S^2\setminus C$, where $C:=\{(x,0,z)\in S^2:x\ge0\}$; $C$ is closed and $\sigma(C)=0$ by applying the integral identity of
[[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]] to its indicator. For $l\ge m\ge0$, define the representative
$\widetilde Y_{lm}:S^2\to\mathbb C$ on $S^2\setminus C$ by
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)):=b_{lm}w_{lm}(\cos\theta)\frac{e^{im\varphi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}},$$
and on the cut $C$ by
$$\widetilde Y_{lm}(\sin\theta,0,\cos\theta):=b_{lm}w_{lm}(\cos\theta)/\sqrt{2\pi}\qquad(0\le\theta\le\pi).$$
The limits at $\varphi=0$ and $2\pi$ agree because $m$ is an integer, and the endpoint values of $w_{lm}$ from (a) give the limits at the poles; hence $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ is continuous. For $1\le m\le l$ set
$\widetilde Y_{l,-m}:=(-1)^m\overline{\widetilde Y_{lm}}$, and write $Y_{lm}$ for the class of $\widetilde Y_{lm}$ in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$. Then:

(a) each $w_{lm}$ extends continuously to $[-1,1]$, with $w_{lm}(\pm1)=0$ when $m\ge1$, and on $(-1,1)$
it satisfies the associated Legendre equation
$$-\bigl((1-t^2)w_{lm}'\bigr)'+\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}w_{lm}=l(l+1)w_{lm}\qquad(-1<t<1),$$
equivalently $(1-t^2)w_{lm}''-2tw_{lm}'+\Bigl[l(l+1)-\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}\Bigr]w_{lm}=0$;

(b) for fixed $m\ge0$ the functions $w_{lm}$, $l\ge m$, are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2((-1,1),dt)$:
$\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}w_{km}\,dt=0$ for $k\ne l$; moreover $0<\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt<+\infty$;

(c) with $b_{lm}:=\bigl(\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt\bigr)^{-1/2}>0$ and the representatives just defined, one has
$|Y_{l,-m}|=|Y_{lm}|$ and
$\overline{Y_{lm}}=(-1)^mY_{l,-m}$ for all $l$ and all $m$ with $|m|\le l$;

(d) the family $\{Y_{lm}:l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l\}$ is orthonormal in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]): for all $(l,m)\ne(l',m')$
with $|m|\le l$, $|m'|\le l'$, the integral $\int_{S^2}Y_{lm}\overline{Y_{l'm'}}\,d\sigma$ equals $0$, and it
equals $1$ when $(l,m)=(l',m')$;

(e) $w_{l0}=P_l$, and $w_{ll}(t)=(-1)^l\frac{(2l)!}{2^l l!}(1-t^2)^{l/2}$.

The functions $Y_{lm}$ are complex-valued $L^2$-functions on the sphere; no physical interpretation as angular
momentum eigenfunctions or spherical harmonics of an atom is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix an integer $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$, let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$ with the
componentwise operators $Q_{j},P_{k}$ and the Schwartz class
$\mathcal S^{(r)}=\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C^{r})$
([[lem-nrqm-kinematics-componentwise-position-and-momentum]],
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]), and let $U(R)$ for $R\in SO(3)$ be
the spatial rotation action of [[lem-nrqm-symmetries-spatial-rotation-action]]
(so that $(U(R)f)(x)=f(R^{-1}x)$ componentwise and $U$ is a strongly continuous
unitary representation). For $i=1,2,3$ define the rotation matrices
$$R_{1}(t):=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&\cos t&-\sin t\\0&\sin t&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_{2}(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&0&\sin t\\0&1&0\\-\sin t&0&\cos t\end{pmatrix},\quad R_{3}(t):=\begin{pmatrix}\cos t&-\sin t&0\\\sin t&\cos t&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},$$
put $U_{i}(t):=U(R_{i}(t))$, and let $L_{i}$ be the self-adjoint operator with
$U_{i}(t)=e^{-itL_{i}/\hbar}$ furnished by Stone's theorem
([[thm-stone-one-parameter-unitary-groups]],
[[def-infinitesimal-generator-of-a-unitary-group]]). Then:

(a) for each $i$ the family $t\mapsto U_{i}(t)$ is a strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary group with $U_{i}(s+t)=U_{i}(s)U_{i}(t)$ and
$U_{i}(0)=\mathrm{id}$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]);

(b) for every $\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}$ the curve $t\mapsto U_{i}(t)\psi$ is
differentiable at $t=0$ into $H^{(r)}$ with
$$\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}U_{i}(t)\psi=-\sum_{j=1}^{3}(e_{i}\times x)_{j}\,D_{j}\psi,$$
and consequently $\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq D(L_{i})$ and
$$L_{i}\psi=-i\hbar\sum_{j=1}^{3}(e_{i}\times x)_{j}D_{j}\psi=\sum_{j,k=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ijk}\,Q_{j}P_{k}\psi\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)});$$

(c) $L_{i}\mathcal S^{(r)}\subseteq\mathcal S^{(r)}$ for each $i$, and on
$\mathcal S^{(r)}$ the commutation relations hold:
$$L_{i}L_{k}\psi-L_{k}L_{i}\psi=i\hbar\sum_{j=1}^{3}\varepsilon_{ikj}\,L_{j}\psi\qquad(\psi\in\mathcal S^{(r)}).$$
(d) For each $i$ the Schwartz class is a core for $L_i$: on $D(L_i)$
the graph norm
$$\|\psi\|_{L_i}:=\bigl(\|\psi\|_{H^{(r)}}^{2}+\hbar^{-2}\|L_i\psi\|_{H^{(r)}}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$$
makes $\mathcal S^{(r)}$ dense in $D(L_i)$ (equivalently, the graph closure of
$L_i|_{\mathcal S^{(r)}}$ is $L_i$). This norm is equivalent to the ordinary
graph norm because $\hbar>0$ is fixed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the
cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$. Let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]
with its componentwise inner product, let $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$ be the
scalar position and momentum operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], and let
$\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^{1}$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Write
$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}\mathcal F_{2}\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$
for its componentwise version, with $\Psi_{0}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a).
Define, componentwise,
$$D(Q_{j}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (Q_{j}f)_{l}:=x_{j}f_{l},$$
$$D(P_{k}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{k}f_{l}\text{ exists in }L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
where $D_{k}$ is the weak derivative of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]].
Write $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the classes whose components
lie in $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]),
and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the componentwise Schwartz
class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]). Then:

(a) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums
$\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]]; in particular
$Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint with the displayed
domains;

(b) $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary,
$$D(P_{k})=\bigl\{f\in H^{(r)}:\ \xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\bigr\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_{k})$
$$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_{k}\,\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi;$$

(c) the componentwise translation $T_{a}^{(r)}f:=f(\cdot-a)$, $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$,
is unitary, leaves $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$,
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$
invariant, satisfies $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ for
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, and
$$T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I,\qquad T_{a}^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(P_{k}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=P_{k};$$

(d) for every $f\in D(P_{j})$,
$$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f \qquad\text{in }H^{(r)},$$
so the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$t\mapsto T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ has generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and
$$T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the exponential being the spectral-calculus flow of the self-adjoint operator
$P_{j}$.

notation of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-orbital-self-adjoint-generators]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-laplacian-diagonal-domain]]: $S^2$ with its

(a) each $L_{i}$ leaves $V_{l}$ invariant, and the restriction

(c) for every $F$ in the finite span $H$ one has

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], a finite Borel measure ([[def-measure]],
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Let

$$\Phi:(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)\to S^2,\qquad \Phi(\theta,\varphi):=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\ \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\ \cos\theta),$$

and let $H:=\{(x,y,0)\in\mathbb R^3:x\ge0\}$ denote the closed half-plane, a Lebesgue-null Borel set
([[thm-affine-hyperplanes-and-proper-subspaces-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]]). Then:

(a) for every Borel function $F:S^2\to[0,+\infty]$,
$$\int_{S^2}F\,d\sigma=\int_{(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)}F\bigl(\Phi(\theta,\varphi)\bigr)\,\sin\theta\ d(\theta,\varphi),$$
the right-hand integral being the Lebesgue integral over the open rectangle;

(b) $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$;

(c) the identity of (a) holds with $F\in L^1(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$ in the sense that $F\circ\Phi$ is Lebesgue
integrable on the rectangle against $\sin\theta\,d(\theta,\varphi)$ and the two integrals agree (real and
imaginary parts, positive and negative parts).

Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the
cited scalar operator and spectral suppliers. Fix integers $d\ge1$, $r\ge1$ and
$\hbar>0$. Let $H^{(r)}=L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ be the
component-valued space of [[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]]
with its componentwise inner product, let $Q_{j}^{(1)},P_{k}^{(1)}$ be the
scalar position and momentum operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ of
[[def-nrqm-magnetic-and-detection-position-and-momentum-operators]], and let
$\mathcal F_{2}$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with
$\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^{1}$
([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Write
$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}:=\Psi_{0}\bigl(\bigoplus_{l}\mathcal F_{2}\bigr)\Psi_{0}^{-1}$
for its componentwise version, with $\Psi_{0}$ the unitary of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-component-valued-wavefunction-identifications]] clause (a).
Define, componentwise,
$$D(Q_{j}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ x_{j}f_{l}\in L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (Q_{j}f)_{l}:=x_{j}f_{l},$$
$$D(P_{k}):=\bigl\{f=(f_{l})\in H^{(r)}:\ D_{k}f_{l}\text{ exists in }L^{2}\ \text{for all }l\bigr\},\qquad (P_{k}f)_{l}:=-i\hbar\,D_{k}f_{l},$$
where $D_{k}$ is the weak derivative of [[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]].
Write $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the classes whose components
lie in $W^{m,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]),
and $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ for the componentwise Schwartz
class ([[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]). Then:

(a) under $\Psi_{0}$ the operators $Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are the orthogonal sums
$\bigoplus_{l}Q_{j}^{(1)}$ and $\bigoplus_{l}P_{k}^{(1)}$ of
[[lem-nrqm-kinematics-orthogonal-sums-of-self-adjoint-operators]]; in particular
$Q_{j}$ and $P_{k}$ are densely defined and self-adjoint with the displayed
domains;

(b) $\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}$ is unitary,
$$D(P_{k})=\bigl\{f\in H^{(r)}:\ \xi_{k}\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f\in L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})\bigr\},$$
and for every $f\in D(P_{k})$
$$\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}(P_{k}f)(\xi)=2\pi\hbar\,\xi_{k}\,\mathcal F_{2}^{(r)}f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi;$$

(c) the componentwise translation $T_{a}^{(r)}f:=f(\cdot-a)$, $a\in\mathbb R^{d}$,
is unitary, leaves $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$,
$W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$
invariant, satisfies $D_{k}(T_{a}^{(r)}f)=T_{a}^{(r)}(D_{k}f)$ for
$f\in W^{1,2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$, and
$$T_{a}^{(r)}D(Q_{j})=D(Q_{j}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}Q_{j}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=Q_{j}-a_{j}I,\qquad T_{a}^{(r)}D(P_{k})=D(P_{k}),\quad T_{a}^{(r)}P_{k}\bigl(T_{a}^{(r)}\bigr)^{-1}=P_{k};$$

(d) for every $f\in D(P_{j})$,
$$\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t\bigl(T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}f-f\bigr)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}f \qquad\text{in }H^{(r)},$$
so the strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group
$t\mapsto T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}$ has generator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}P_{j}$ and
$$T_{te_{j}}^{(r)}=\exp\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tP_{j}\Bigr)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the exponential being the spectral-calculus flow of the self-adjoint operator
$P_{j}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A finite-valued function $f=u+iv:X\to\mathbb C$ is **measurable** when $u,v$ are real measurable functions. Write
$$N_p(f)=\begin{cases}\left(\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p},&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty,\\+\infty,&\displaystyle\int_X|f|^p\,d\mu=+\infty,\end{cases}\quad(1\le p<\infty),\qquad N_\infty(f)=\inf\{M\in[0,\infty]:|f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}.$$
The finite case uses the real power; the infinite case is assigned directly,
so $N_p(f)$ is defined for every measurable finite-valued complex $f$.
The infimum of the empty set of finite bounds is $\infty$; equivalently allow $M=\infty$. Define $\mathcal L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\{f:f\text{ measurable},N_p(f)<\infty\}$ and its **set quotient** $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)=\mathcal L^p/\!\sim$, where $f\sim g$ means $f=g$ a.e. This extends [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]. Norm and vector-space assertions are established separately.

Here $|u+iv|=\sqrt{u^2+v^2}$ and $\overline{u+iv}=u-iv$ as in [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. These operations preserve measurability: $u^2+v^2$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and
$$\{|f|>a\}=\begin{cases}\{u^2+v^2>a^2\},&a\ge0,\\X,&a<0.\end{cases}$$
Thus [[thm-threshold-characterisations-of-real-and-extended-real-measurability]] applies. For $g=a+ib$, the formulas $fg=(ua-vb)+i(ub+va)$ and $\overline f=u-iv$ prove the remaining claims by real arithmetic closure. Nonnegative powers are measurable because $\{r^t>b\}=\{r>b^{1/t}\}$ for $r\ge0,t>0,b\ge0$, with the negative thresholds automatic.

A **finite simple** complex function has finite range and measurable fibers. Its **finite-measure support** condition is $\mu(\{s\ne0\})<\infty$. This concerns the nonzero set, not compactness of its closure. The zero function is an admissible finite simple function, including when $X=\varnothing$ or $\mu(X)=0$.

Integration is componentwise: for integrable $f=u+iv$,
$$\int f\,d\mu=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$
This is the earlier convention of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]] and [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]. The inequalities $|u|,|v|\le|f|\le|u|+|v|$ show that integrability of the modulus and integrability of both components are equivalent.

For $n\ge1$, define complex $C_c(\mathbb R^n)$, $C_0(\mathbb R^n)$ and $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ by requiring both components to lie in the corresponding real spaces ([[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]], [[def-c-zero-on-rn]]). Derivatives are componentwise, with the multi-index and all-ordered-partials conventions of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. The union of the two compact component supports is compact. A measurable complex $f$ is **locally integrable** for Lebesgue measure if $\int_K|f|<\infty$ on every compact $K$. The component inequalities give the equivalent componentwise condition. By [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], closed bounded balls are compact and each compact set is bounded. Hence compact integrability implies integrability on every bounded open ball by restriction from its closure; conversely each compact set is contained in a bounded open ball. These prove both directions of the ball formulation.

For a topological $X$ with Borel sets contained in $\mathcal A$, define
$$\operatorname{ess\,supp}_\mu f=X\setminus\bigcup\{U:U\text{ open and }f=0\text{ a.e. on }U\}.$$
Changing $f$ on one measurable null set preserves the zero-a.e. property on every $U$, since the union of that set and the old exceptional set is null. Thus essential support depends only on the a.e. class. Ordinary support means $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}$ and can change with the representative.

For the following illustration assume [[def-countable-choice]]. For $f=\mathbf1_{\mathbb Q}$ on $\mathbb R$, [[prop-countable-subsets-of-rn-are-lebesgue-null]] gives $f=0$ Lebesgue-a.e.; therefore $N_\infty(f)=0$ and $\operatorname{ess\,supp}f=\varnothing$, since $U=\mathbb R$ occurs in the union. But [[lem-q-and-irrationals-dense-r]] gives $\overline{\{f\ne0\}}=\mathbb R$. For the Dirac probability measure at zero ([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), the bound $1$ holds everywhere and every $0\le M<1$ fails on $\{0\}$, of measure one. Thus $N_{\infty,\delta_0}(f)=1$.

The raw $L^2$ pairing convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$, linear in the first variable. Its integrability and class invariance are obligations of the later pairing items. **Bilinear tests** instead use $\int fs$, with no conjugation of $s$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

e0$ and each $i$, the product rule gives $(x	imes
abla)_{i}\psi=R(|x|)(D_{i}h_{lm})(x)w$ because $(x	imes
abla)_{i}R(|x|)=R'(|x|)\,(x	imes x)_{i}/|x|=0$, and by [F1] the function $-i\hbar D_{i}h_{lm}$ is the polynomial representative of $L_{i}^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}$; moreover [F1] gives $D_{3}h_{lm}=im\,h_{lm}$.

[Core action and $L_{3}$ eigenvalue] By step 1.1 and [F2], $\psi\in D(L_{i})$ and $L_{i}\psi=\sum_{j,k}\varepsilon_{ijk}Q_{j}P_{k}\psi=-i\hbar\,(x\times\nabla)_{i}\psi=R(|x|)\,(-i\hbar D_{i}h_{lm})(x)\,w$ for almost every $x$, where the weak derivatives agree with the classical ones by [F5]; here $P_{k}=-i\hbar\partial_{k}$ on the Schwartz class, so the factor $-i\hbar$ occurs once. For $i=3$, [F1] gives $L_{3}\psi=-i\hbar R\,D_{3}h_{lm}\,w=\hbar mR\,h_{lm}w=\hbar m\psi$, proving (a).

[Norms and the Casimir form] Put $q_i:=D_i h_{lm}$. Each term $x_j\partial_k h_{lm}$ is homogeneous of degree $l$ or zero, so $q_i(r\Omega)=r^lq_i(\Omega)$ for $r>0$; for $l=0$, $q_i=0$. By step 2.1, $\|w\|=1$ and polar integration [F4], $\|L_i\psi\|^2=\hbar^2\int_{\mathbb R^3}|R(|x|)|^2|q_i(x)|^2\,dx=\hbar^2\bigl(\int_0^\infty|R(r)|^2r^{2l+2}\,dr\bigr)\int_{S^2}|q_i(\Omega)|^2\,d\sigma(\Omega)$. By [F1], $L_i^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}=-i\hbar q_i|_{S^2}$, hence $\|L_i\psi\|^2=\|R\|_l^2\|L_i^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}\|^2$. Likewise homogeneity of $h_{lm}$ and [F4] give $\|\psi\|^2=\|R\|_l^2\int_{S^2}|Y_{lm}|^2\,d\sigma=\|R\|_l^2$, using the normalization in [[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] clause (d). Finally, on the finite invariant block $V_l$, self-adjointness and [F3] give $\sum_i\|L_i^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}\|^2=\langle\sum_i(L_i^{\mathrm{sph}})^2Y_{lm},Y_{lm}\rangle=\hbar^2l(l+1)$, so $\sum_i\|L_i\psi\|^2=\hbar^2l(l+1)\|\psi\|^2$, proving (b), including $l=0$ and $R=0$.

[Readings] Let $R\not\equiv0$ and put $\varphi:=\psi/\|\psi\|$; by step 2.1, $L_{3}\varphi=\hbar m\varphi$ with $\varphi\in D(L_{3})$, so the mean and the second moment of the law of $L_{3}$ in the pure preparation $[\varphi]$ are $\langle L_{3}\varphi,\varphi\rangle=\hbar m$ and $\|L_{3}\varphi\|^{2}=\hbar^{2}m^{2}$, with variance $0$; for each $i$, step 2.1 gives $\varphi\in D(L_{i})$ and step 3.1 gives $\|L_{i}\varphi\|^{2}=\|L_{i}^{\mathrm{sph}}Y_{lm}\|^{2}$, so the mean and second moment of the law of $L_{i}$ are finite with that second moment, and the quadratic form is $\sum_{i}\|L_{i}\varphi\|^{2}=\hbar^{2}l(l+1)$, which is (c).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).
